name: Bahamas
summary: An archipelago of about 700 islands, where Columbus first landed in 1492; British until 1973; now a tourism and banking centre.

knownFor.label: Columbus’s landfall
knownFor.note: First landing in the Americas, probably San Salvador.

knownFor.label: Junkanoo
knownFor.note: Street festival with costumes and drums.

location.value: Islands north of Cuba; about 10,010 km² of land (13,880 km² including water).

terrain.value: About 700 low, flat limestone islands and cays, with coral reefs and shallow seas.

climate.value: Subtropical, with a hurricane season and warm winters.

disasters.value: Hurricane Dorian (2019) caused catastrophic damage to Abaco and Grand Bahama.

urbanisation.value: Nassau, on New Providence, holds about two-thirds of the population.

disease.value: Dengue occurs, and health care is good for the region.

migration.value: Large emigration to the UK, US and Canada.

economicBase.value: Tourism and offshore financial services (about 15% of GDP).

tradeRoutes.value: Nassau is a major cruise port, and Freeport handles cargo.

wealth.value: Among the wealthiest countries in the Americas.

moneyAndTax.value: The Bahamian dollar; no income, corporate, capital gains or wealth tax.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a Commonwealth member.

keyRulers.value: Lynden Pindling: the first black premier (1967) and first prime minister; unseated in 1992.

succession.value: Elections to the House of Assembly choose the prime minister.

stability.value: A stable democracy since independence in 1973.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Royal Bahamas Defence Force, with 26 patrol craft and over 1,100 personnel.

majorWars.value: The islands were a pirate base in the early 1700s until Woodes Rogers restored British rule in 1718.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Commonwealth and CARICOM; close ties with the United States.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Schools; University of the West Indies campuses nearby.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Small planes and boats link the many islands, and Nassau has a busy airport.

languageWriting.value: English is official; Bahamian Creole, an English-based creole, is also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Junkanoo, an Afro-Bahamian street parade held in Nassau.

socialStructure.value: Mostly of African descent, from people enslaved on sugar plantations.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared island and Caribbean identity, with a strong culture of Junkanoo festival parades.

dailyLife.value: Houses; fish, breadfruit, rice and peas.

neighbours.value: Lies southeast of Florida and north of Cuba.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity; slavery was abolished across the British Empire on 1 August 1834.

colonisation.value: A British crown colony from 1718 (set up to end piracy) until independence in 1973.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: The Bahamas continue as an independent state.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
